      POSCO v. United States (opens in a new tab)
      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cit-1_24-cv-00006 / USCOURTS-cit-1_24-cv-00006-0

      FAPD-AI: In POSCO v. United States, Court No. 24-00006, filed August 8, 2025, Judge Jane A. Restani of the Court of International Trade partially sustained and partially remanded the Commerce Department's final determination in a countervailing duty administrative review of certain carbon and alloy steel cut-to-length plate from the Republic of Korea. The determination found a 0.87 percent subsidy rate for POSCO based on Korea's electricity provision and its Cap and Trade Law. The portion of the opinion provided holds that Commerce acted unreasonably in grouping the Korean steel industry with two unrelated industries in its de facto specificity analysis of the electricity subsidy. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    • Observed at 19:39:50 Eastern time ET
      POSCO v. United States (opens in a new tab)
      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cit-1_24-cv-00006 / USCOURTS-cit-1_24-cv-00006-1

      FAPD-AI: In this April 17, 2026 Opinion and Order, the U.S. Court of International Trade sustained in part and remanded in part the Department of Commerce's final remand redetermination in the countervailing duty administrative review of certain carbon and alloy steel cut-to-length plate from the Republic of Korea for the 2021 period of review. The court sustained Commerce's findings except the specificity finding regarding the allocation of extra Korea Allowance Units (KAUs), which it remanded. The court also noted that Commerce had found the Korean electricity subsidy was not shown to be de facto specific on remand. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    • Observed at 19:39:50 Eastern time ET
      POSCO v. United States (opens in a new tab)
      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cit-1_24-cv-00006 / USCOURTS-cit-1_24-cv-00006-2

      FAPD-AI: In this October 27, 2026 Opinion and Order, the U.S. Court of International Trade sustained Commerce's second remand redetermination in the same countervailing duty review of carbon and alloy steel cut-to-length plate from Korea. Commerce had determined on remand that the allocation of KAUs is de facto specific under 19 U.S.C. § 1677(5A)(D)(iii)(I), comparing 494 recipients to 906,325 companies within the Government of Korea's jurisdiction. Plaintiffs POSCO and the Government of the Republic of Korea argued that the comparison used an improper denominator, and the court sustained Commerce's determination. USCOURTS-SEL-02

    In re Raj K. Patel (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-cit-1_26-cv-04703 / USCOURTS-cit-1_26-cv-04703-0

    FAPD-AI: In this October 27, 2026 Opinion and Order, the U.S. Court of International Trade dismissed the complaint of pro se plaintiff Raj K. Patel for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. The complaint alleged violations of international trade agreements and due-process protections related to access to certain medical technologies, and sought declaratory relief and $380 million in damages. The court denied Patel's motion to compel acceptance of the complaint as moot, finding that the cited trade agreements are not laws falling within the court's residual jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i). USCOURTS-SEL-02

    FAPD-AI: In an opinion filed October 28, 2026, the First Circuit in Wright v. United Services Automobile Association, No. 25-1979, on appeal from the District of Massachusetts, held that Massachusetts law rather than the federal filed rate doctrine governs whether policyholders may sue their motor vehicle insurers under Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A over rates approved by the Massachusetts Insurance Commissioner. The court certified the state-law questions to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, and the excerpt provided is truncated. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    In re: Wenkman (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca13-26-01424 / USCOURTS-ca13-26-01424-0

    FAPD-AI: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's rejection of all pending claims (1-20) of U.S. Patent Application No. 18/424,833, which relates to a computer-implemented method for bartering groceries and other goods for silver and gold. The court agreed that representative claim 1 is directed to the abstract idea of a fundamental economic practice under 35 U.S.C. § 101. The appeal also challenged the Board's written-description rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 18:40:37 Eastern time ET
    Gurmit Kahlon v. Attorney General United States of America (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-25-02681 / USCOURTS-ca3-25-02681-0

    FAPD-AI: The Third Circuit denied the petition for review filed by Gurmit Singh Kahlon of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision that affirmed the denial of withholding of removal based on religion and political opinion. The court found that substantial evidence supported the finding that Gurmit Singh Kahlon did not show a clear probability of persecution if returned to India. The court also held that the Board did not abuse its discretion in denying the motion to remand for failure to include the adjustment-of-status application required by 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(c)(1). USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 18:40:37 Eastern time ET
    Marquis Robinson v. Self Help Movement, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca3-26-01838 / USCOURTS-ca3-26-01838-0

    FAPD-AI: In a non-precedential per curiam opinion filed October 28, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed the Eastern District of Pennsylvania's grant of summary judgment to the defendants in Marquis Robinson v. Self Help Movement, et al. The court held that a supervisor's isolated requests that the plaintiff lift her back did not meet the severe or pervasive standard for hostile work environment harassment under Title VII and the PHRA. The court also held that Robinson's race-based claims concerning outside work offers and a client's racial slur were not exhausted because they fell outside the scope of his EEOC charge, and it denied his motion to file supplemental documents. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 18:40:36 Eastern time ET
    United States v. Lerblance (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-07095 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-07095-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit dismissed the appeal of Andrew Frank Lerblance, who pled guilty to distribution of methamphetamine and received an 84-month sentence followed by four years of supervised release, and granted counsel's motion to withdraw. The court found that the appeal falls within the scope of a written appeal waiver, that the waiver was knowing and voluntary, and that enforcing it would not result in a miscarriage of justice. The court concluded that the appeal is wholly frivolous. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Contreras Ramirez, et al v. Blanche (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca10-25-09577 / USCOURTS-ca10-25-09577-0

    FAPD-AI: The Tenth Circuit denied the pro se petition for review filed by Maria Alejandra Contreras Ramirez, Rodrigo Andres Gonzalez Mosquera, and their minor child, who challenged the Board of Immigration Appeals' affirmance of the denial of withholding of removal.     Kelvin Smith v. Kohler Co., et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-03248 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-03248-0

    FAPD-AI: In Kelvin Smith v. Kohler Co., et al., No. 25-3248, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the dismissal with prejudice of a pro se complaint alleging religious discrimination under Title VII based on a COVID-19 testing requirement. The court held that the amended complaint did not connect the objection to the testing requirement to a religious belief or practice, and that the district court could dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(b) after the plaintiff failed to file a second amended complaint as ordered. The court also held that a pro se litigant cannot represent other parties or a putative class, and that the district court acted within its discretion in declining to consider untimely and noncompliant filings. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    Patricia Tillman v. Illinois State Board of Elections, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-26-01108 / USCOURTS-ca7-26-01108-0

    FAPD-AI: In Patricia Tillman v. Illinois State Board of Elections, et al., No. 26-1108, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the dismissal for failure to state a claim of a 42 U.S.C. § 1983 complaint challenging the Board's disqualification of a candidate from the March 2026 primary ballot. The court held that the plaintiff received notice and an opportunity to be heard in the Board proceedings, and that she did not plausibly allege an inadequate post-deprivation remedy because she voluntarily dismissed her state-court challenge. The court also held that the district court did not abuse its discretion by failing to order amendment sua sponte. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    USA v. Kevin Cooper (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-26-01123 / USCOURTS-ca7-26-01123-0

    FAPD-AI: In United States v. Kevin M. Cooper, No. 26-1123, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the denial of a third motion for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A). The court held that a nonretroactive change in law does not constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason under Rutherford v. United States, 146 S. Ct. 1320 (2026), and that the medical conditions and other arguments presented were insufficient to support release. The court also noted that, having found no extraordinary and compelling reason, the district court was not required to determine the extent of any reduction under the sentencing factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a). USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:39:18 Eastern time ET
    Calvin McMillan v. National Football League, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-26-01957 / USCOURTS-ca7-26-01957-0

    FAPD-AI: In Calvin McMillan v. National Football League, et al., No. 26-1957, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) of a copyright infringement complaint alleging that lottery ticket phrases copied lyrics from two songs about the Green Bay Packers. The court held that the plaintiff did not prove registration of the works and that the short phrases at issue, including Pack Attack, Pack Is Back, and Go Pack Go, are slogan-like combinations of ordinary words that are not protected by copyright under 37 C.F.R. § 202.1(a). The court also noted that the antitrust claims in the complaint were not pursued on appeal. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    USA v. George Sisk (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-01499 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-01499-0

    FAPD-AI: The Seventh Circuit granted appointed counsel's motion to withdraw and dismissed the appeal of George Sisk, who pleaded guilty without a plea agreement to Hobbs Act robbery, a firearm offense under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), and felon-in-possession under § 922(g)(1). Sisk was sentenced to an aggregate 156-month prison term, and the court's order, issued under Anders v. California, found no nonfrivolous issues for appeal. The order addresses the constitutionality of § 922(g)(1), the Rule 11 plea colloquy, competency, the denial of pre-plea motions, sentence reasonableness, and an ineffective-assistance claim reserved for collateral review.     USA v. Troy Burke (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca7-25-02512 / USCOURTS-ca7-25-02512-0

    FAPD-AI: The Seventh Circuit affirmed the conviction of Troy D. Burke for bank robbery under 18 U.S.C. § 2113(a) and his 20-year sentence, which was the statutory maximum. Burke argued that the evidence was insufficient, particularly the accuracy of GPS tracking device data tied to marked cash he received from a teller. The court found that testimony from the teller, the credit union president, and the arresting officer, along with photographs and surveillance video, was sufficient for a rational trier of fact to find him guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. The order is nonprecedential. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    FAPD-AI: The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the defendants in Steven Ingalls, Jr.'s 42 U.S.C. § 1983 action alleging Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference to his medical needs. The defendants were Centurion Health of Indiana, LLC, Dr. Samuel Byrd, and grievance specialist Shelby Crichfield at Wabash Valley Correctional Facility. The court held that the record showed Dr. Byrd exercised medical judgment, that no Centurion policy or practice violation was established, and that Crichfield's rejection of a grievance as untimely did not show deliberate indifference.     FAPD-AI: In Candie Yer Herr v. Helen M. Ludwig, No. 25-3093, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the dismissal of a petition for a writ of mandamus under 28 U.S.C. § 1361 that sought to compel actions by a Chapter 7 bankruptcy trustee. The court held that private Chapter 7 trustees are not federal officers or employees and therefore are not subject to § 1361.     Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-20488 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-20488-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed October 28, 2026, the Fifth Circuit vacated one special condition of supervised release imposed on Valentin Martinez-Ornelas following his methamphetamine sentence and remanded for conforming changes to the written judgment.   • Observed at 16:39:16 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Patton (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca5-25-20494 / USCOURTS-ca5-25-20494-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed October 28, 2026, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the bench-trial convictions of Kelvin Patton for Hobbs Act robbery under 18 U.S.C. § 1951 and for brandishing a firearm during a crime of violence under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), along with the 146-month sentence. The court held that the robbery of cash belonging to a Denny's restaurant satisfied the interstate commerce element because the business purchased out-of-state goods, that only a de minimis effect on interstate commerce is required, and that the intended victim's identity was not relevant to that element. The court also held that the denial of a U.S.S.G. § 3E1.1 acceptance-of-responsibility reduction was not without foundation, because the defendant challenged the sufficiency of the evidence on an element of the offense. USCOURTS-SEL-01

Cook raised facial Second Amendment and Commerce Clause challenges to § 922(g)(1) for the first time on appeal, conceded that circuit precedent foreclosed both, and asked the court to hold the appeal in abeyance pending the en banc decision in United States v.     Josue Batista v. Michael Saba (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-26-10458 / USCOURTS-ca11-26-10458-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed October 28, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit reviewed the appeal of pro se plaintiff Josue Batista from the Southern District of Florida's dismissal with prejudice of his second amended complaint against Michael Saba, which alleged race discrimination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, and from the denial of his Rule 59(e) motion. The court held that the complaint did not plausibly allege intentional race-based discrimination, that the § 1982 claim was properly dismissed and not improperly merged into the § 1981 analysis, and that further amendment would be futile. The court vacated the dismissal in part and remanded so the district court can first consider whether any retaliation claims were raised and plausibly alleged, affirmed in part, and denied Saba's motion for sanctions. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    US v. Raymond Aigbekaen (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca4-26-06420 / USCOURTS-ca4-26-06420-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam decision issued October 28, 2026, the Fourth Circuit affirmed orders of the District of Maryland in United States v. Raymond Idemudia Aigbekaen. The district court had granted in part a 28 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) compassionate release motion, reducing the sentence by six months, and had later denied a motion for reconsideration and a subsequent compassionate release motion. The court found no reversible error, denied the appellant's motion for transcripts, denied as moot his motion for bail or release pending appeal, and declined to hold oral argument. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:39:14 Eastern time ET
    USA v. Johnson Saint-Louis (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-13084 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-13084-0

    FAPD-AI: The Eleventh Circuit, in an unpublished per curiam opinion, affirmed the convictions of Johnson Saint-Louis for armed bank robbery under 18 U.S.C. § 2113(a) and (d) and for brandishing a firearm under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A)(ii), and vacated the sentence and remanded for resentencing. The appellant argued cumulative trial error based on prosecutorial closing argument and insufficient identity evidence, that the armed-bank-robbery statute does not qualify as a crime of violence under § 924(c), and that a two-level physical restraint enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2B3.1(b)(4)(B) was improperly applied. The opinion describes a February 2021 robbery of a Bank of America ATM in Longwood, Florida, and a sentence of 87 months on Count 1 plus a consecutive 84 months on Count 2. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    • Observed at 16:39:14 Eastern time ET
      Nancy Salas v. Monsanto Company (opens in a new tab)
      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-14030 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-14030-0

      FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam order, the Eleventh Circuit granted Monsanto Company's unopposed motion for summary affirmance and affirmed a final judgment against it on Nancy Salas's Florida state-law negligent failure-to-warn claim concerning Roundup. The court held that its earlier decision in Carson v. Monsanto Co., 92 F.4th 980 (11th Cir. 2024), controls, concluding that the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) did not preempt the claim. The court reasoned that Florida law, like Georgia law, requires pesticide manufacturers to warn users of potential health and safety risks, paralleling FIFRA. USCOURTS-SEL-01

    • Observed at 16:39:14 Eastern time ET
      Nancy Salas v. Monsanto Company (opens in a new tab)
      Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-24-14030 / USCOURTS-ca11-24-14030-1

      FAPD-AI: On remand from the Supreme Court, the Eleventh Circuit granted the parties' joint motion for summary adjudication and reversed the district court's judgment against Monsanto Company in the Nancy Salas case. The Supreme Court had granted certiorari, vacated the prior Eleventh Circuit judgment, and remanded for further consideration in light of Monsanto Co. v. Durnell, 609 U.S. 371 (2026). Applying Durnell, the court held that Salas's state common law failure-to-warn claim is preempted by federal law. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 16:39:14 Eastern time ET
    Cyrille Beckodro v. John Doe 1, et al (opens in a new tab)
    Judicial opinion · govinfo API · USCOURTS-ca11-25-12140 / USCOURTS-ca11-25-12140-0

    FAPD-AI: In an unpublished per curiam opinion, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of pro se plaintiff Cyrille Kouambo Beckodro's second motion for relief under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b), which sought reconsideration of the dismissal of his civil complaint against John Doe defendants. The court found no abuse of discretion under Rule 60(b)(2), because the appellant did not show that the newly discovered evidence would be material or would change the basis for dismissal, and under Rule 60(b)(6), because no extraordinary circumstances were shown. The underlying complaint alleged stalking, noise-based harassment, delayed postal deliveries, and discrimination by a university bursar's office, and the district court had dismissed it for failure to state a claim. USCOURTS-SEL-01

  • Observed at 09:58:37 Eastern time ET
    Public Law 119–135: To convey the reversionary interest of the United States in certain land in Sacramento, California. (opens in a new tab)
    Enacted law · govinfo API · PLAW-119publ135

    FAPD-AI: Public Law 119-135, approved October 22, 2026 (H.R. 952), is known as the Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act. It directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Bureau of Land Management, to offer and convey the United States reversionary interest in approximately 8.43 acres in Sacramento, California, to the owner of record of the adjoining parcels within two years of a buyer's request, for not less than fair market value and subject to valid existing rights. The buyer pays the appraised value plus all related costs, and the proceeds are deposited in the Federal Land Disposal Account. The Act also preserves a right-of-way of at least 50 feet on each side of the Southern Pacific Transportation Company main track centerline and does not confirm any adverse possession, prescription, or abandonment claims. PLAW-SEL-01

  • Observed at 09:58:37 Eastern time ET
    Public Law 119–136: To provide for the transmission of emergency alerts by satellite, and for other purposes. (opens in a new tab)
    Enacted law · govinfo API · PLAW-119publ136

    FAPD-AI: Public Law 119-136, approved October 22, 2026 (H.R. 7022), is known as the Mystic Alerts Act. It requires covered commercial mobile service providers to file an election with the Federal Communications Commission on whether they will transmit emergency alerts by satellite, and sets deadlines for the Commission to publish a notice of proposed rulemaking within 6 months and a final rule within 18 months, in consultation with the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA. The Act sets the rule's effective date as the later of 36 months after Federal Register publication or 12 months after DHS and FEMA implement the necessary alert-origination standards, and prohibits providers from imposing a separate charge for satellite alert transmission. It also limits liability for covered providers that transmit satellite alerts and meet the Act's obligations, and defines a covered service provider as one that voluntarily elects to transmit alerts under the Warning, Alert, and Response Network Act and offers satellite voice and data service. PLAW-SEL-01

    official summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) is proposing to approve the State of Tennessee's attainment plan for the Sullivan County Nonattainment Area (Sullivan County Area or Area) for the 2010 Sulfur Dioxide (SO 2 ) National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). Additionally, the EPA is proposing to determine that the Area has attained the 2010 SO 2 NAAQS and to approve Tennessee's maintenance plan for continued attainment. With these approvals, the EPA is proposing to approve Tennessee's comprehensive source-specific SO 2 permitted limits for two facilities in the Area, other control measures, and provisions for Reasonably Available Control Measures (RACM) and Reasonably Available Control Technology (RACT), reasonable further progress (RFP), a modeling demonstration of SO 2 attainment and maintenance, and to approve Tennessee's request to redesignate the Area from nonattainment to attainment of the 2010 SO 2 NAAQS. The EPA is taking these actions in accordance with the Clean Air Act (CAA or Act). FR-SEL-02

    Federal Register · govinfo API · ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY · FR-2026-10-29 / 2026-22082

    official summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing amendments to the New Source Performance Standards and Emission Guidelines for the Crude Oil and Natural Gas Source Category to address additional concerns raised with prior regulatory amendments finalized in March 2024. Specifically, the EPA is proposing changes in response to certain petitions for reconsideration of the March 2024 amendments, changes based on policy decisions and supporting legal interpretations, and changes that correct and clarify the regulatory text of the new source performance standards and emission guidelines. First, the EPA proposes to rescind the Super Emitter Program. Second, the EPA proposes to subcategorize different types of well sites affected and designated facilities to address issues related to the requirements finalized in March 2024 for marginal well sites and conventional well sites. Third, the EPA proposes changes to address issues related to liquids unloading, process controllers, pumps, fugitive emissions, storage vessels, covers and closed vent systems, equipment leaks at gas plants, and associated gas.     Alaska Underground Injection Control (UIC) Program; Class VI Primacy (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY · FR-2026-10-29 / 2026-22085

    official summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or the Agency) has received a complete Underground Injection Control (UIC) application from the State of Alaska, requesting primary enforcement responsibility (primacy) for Class VI injection wells under Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) section 1422. The EPA's approval of the State's UIC program primacy application would allow the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission (AOGCC) to issue and enforce compliance with UIC Class VI permits for injection wells used for geologic carbon sequestration. In this action, the EPA proposes to approve Alaska's application to implement the UIC program for Class VI injection wells located within the State, except those located within Indian country and those located within areas of exclusive Federal jurisdiction. FR-SEL-02

    Pleasure Vessels of Malta Entitled To Cruising Licenses (opens in a new tab)
    Federal Register · govinfo API · DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY · FR-2026-10-29 / 2026-22089

    official summary: This document amends U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations by adding the Republic of Malta (Malta) to the list of countries whose pleasure vessels may be issued U.S. cruising licenses. The U.S. Department of State has notified CBP that yachts used and employed exclusively as pleasure vessels and belonging to any resident of the United States are allowed to arrive at and depart from Maltese ports, and to cruise in Maltese waters without complying with formal entry and clearance procedures. Therefore, CBP is extending reciprocal cruising privileges to Maltese-flagged pleasure vessels. FR-SEL-01
